The graph indicates that higher the unemployment rate %, the higher the youth unemployment rate, showing an expected, direct relationship. We can see with Eswatini who has the highest unemployment rate of 22% has the highest youth unemployment rate of 51% as well. There's also Australia which has the second lowest unemployment rate of 3.7% and lowest youth unemployment % of 10.8%. This shows the direct relationship. This occurs because the unemployment rate is measured by those in the labour force under the unemployed people (unemployed / labour force x 100). The labour force contains youth, out of education who is willing and seeking jobs, so higher percentage of labour force employed, higher number of youth employed, especially if they are the majority of the labour force i.e. lack of elderly people. However, there's an exception with Kuwait which has the lowest unemployment rate of 2.2% but a relatively higher youth unemployment rate of 25.5, higher than Australia's despite having an overall lower unemployment. This may be due to a lack of jobs for youth arising as its filled by elderly people; or due to lack of educated youth who don't have the qualifications necessary to gain jobs despite willing and seeking one.

text: Firstly, workers may benefit from moving to the private sector firms as it often offers higher wages than public sector SOEs and government owned businesses as they want to keep their workers motivated and productive, so the firm can increase quality of their service and output thereby being internationally competitive. This allows workers to gain higher disposable income, ability to purchase more basic necessities, goods and services of high quality and thereby have higher living standards. Especially if they work in large businesses or MNCs with a good reputation. They may also benefit from training as private sectors have a higher incentive to profit maximise than state owned enterprises (SOEs). This will increase their skills and labour occupational mobility if a firm closes down, so they can easily switch jobs, reducing potential cyclical or structural unemployment, ensuring they have high living standards. Moreover, they may specialise in a task, through division of labour thats more prominent in private sectors, increasing output and income if they are paid by piece, increased productivity leading to higher income. However, private sectors don't provide pensions like public jobs, so people need to work longer to gain enough savings to maintain their living standards at old age, lowering their quality of life. Furthermore, they have less job security as SOEs try to have low unemployment, while private sectors may switch to capital intensive production, raising unemployment, especially in the long term as workers may gain less training than in public, increasing poverty, lowering living standards.

Firstly a new port may benefit an economy as it would increase job opportunities, lower unemployment rate and maximise the use of their resources such as labor and land, thereby create higher output than before thus face economic growth through higher GDP. It will also increase peoples disposable incomes, increasing ability to spend on goods and services thereby lower absolute poverty and increase living standards. Moreover, it allows and incentivises firms to sell goods abroad, in foreign markets, increasing profits and being able to diversify, expand and consequently further increase job opportunities. It will also increase exports in the country, potentially reducing a BOP current account deficit, and increase government tax revenue through indirect taxes, allowing them to spend on education. It also allows higher imports and foreign firms to set up, increasing competition, lowering prices and increasing consumer choices, thereby raising living standards. However, it may not be beneficial if it increases social and external costs as transporting higher quantity of imports and exports will cause pollution, damage the environment and potentially endanger fish stocks. This will also harm the health of people living nearby, lowering life expectancy and living standards.

A fall in the inflation rate is a fall in inflation which means a fall in the rate of the sustained increase of the average price of goods and services within a period of time. Its also known as disinflation.

Firstly, households may save money in a bank to gain a reward from high interest rates so they can increase their money and savings in the long-term, allowing them to potentially buy something expensive. This is especially the case for target savers who may want to buy a car or house through cash than a mortgage in the future or want higher income to be able to afford it. Households may save contractually by saving a percentage of their income for pensions, especially if working in the private sector, as it may be legally mandated. This is their retirement fund they're saving, and benefiting from interest especially in times of economic uncertainty; allowing them to still purchase goods and services when they're retired, maintaining their living standards.

Firstly, a fall in the foreign exchange rate means the country's value of money has depreciated or fallen in value against another. This makes imports more expensive. If a country is dependent on the imports of raw materials such as oil, coal and steel, to make consumer or capital goods, the costs of production will increase. This is because the variable costs have increased significantly so if a firm wants to maintain their profit margin, especially if they have aim of profit maximisation, they'll raise the prices of goods and services provided. This leads to cost-push inflation as higher imported raw material costs raised price of products. Moreover, the imports of essentials such as rice or wheat may also become expensive and if there's not enough domestic substitutes and alternatives, especially if PED is inelastic, it will also raise prices of necessities, leading to inflation. It may cause a wage spiral as people's real incomes aren't buying as much necessities, bargaining for higher wages which further increases production costs and higher prices onto customers if productivity doesn't increase despite higher pay. This further increases cost-push inflation.
ticks: higher imported raw material costs raised price

text: Firstly, lower bank lending will lower money supply in the economy showing a contractionary monetary policy, it may be beneficial. This will lower people's/households ability to borrow, lowering their disposable income as they can't take loans to buy cars or mortgages/houses so they have lower ability to spend, especially if prices of goods and services are high. This will lower aggregate demand so less expenditure, so firms may reduce prices as they want to maintain sales to not go bankrupt, lowering demand-pull inflation which is beneficial for an economy. Moreover, reduced bank lending by a small proportion will not be significantly harmful as majority of households and firms will still be able to borrow and maintain their living standards. Furthermore, reduced lending reduces firms ability to gain loans for investment in capital or to purchase raw resources by using loans as a working capital in order to not go illiquid/insolvent. This may force firms to be more productive, increasing efficiency in the production process so there's a good allocation of resources ensuring maximum output. This is because if firms are running inefficiently as they rely on loans, lower lending will incentivise them to reduce production costs, increase profits, lowering need for loans. This makes them more productive, potentially increasing quality of output, thereby internationally competitive. However reduced bank lending reduces households, especially low income ones to gain bank loans like overdrafts to purchase basic necessities like shelter and education, lowering living standards and increasing absolute poverty. This gives the economy a poor reputation. Moreover, firms can't borrow loans to purchase advanced capital or train workers to have a productive production process, reducing potential higher profits and expansion which would've increased job opportunities and living standards. If they could've borrowed and spent on development of new products or investment more, the firms may have been more internationally competitive through lower cost production process with low prices and high quality. It reduces potential higher exports and BOP surplus. It also reduces incentive and ability to invest or start a new firm, reducing potential start ups of infant industries which could've grown to be a strategic one or internationally competitive with high profits and corporate tax revenue to governments which could've been spent on higher education, increasing productive potential of the country. Finally, lower lending reduces attractiveness for MNCs to set up, lowering potential higher employment rate and living standards.

text: An economic good is a capital good that can be used to make other consumer or capital goods and services. It has an opportunity cost to produce as it needs resources from four factors of production and isn't a free good like sunlight. It may be a car or machinery.

text: A government may encourage clothes firms to merge to reduce duplication of resources such as electricity lines, allowing for higher productive potential in the economy as resources can be allocated more efficiently and for other uses, increasing overall output of the economy. They may also be able to increase market share by removing competitors if both of the clothes firms are manufacturers, a horizontal merger, allowing them to increase output and sales. This allows the clothes firm to grow and take greater advantage of economies of scale such as managerial as they can use their combined large finances and retained profits to hire specialist managers who increase productivity of the firm. This in turn lowers average production costs, allowing them higher profits and ability to invest in R&D and innovation, increasing quality of products made at lower outputs. They may also develop new products. This will increase consumer choices and living standards; it also increases international competitiveness so the economy may benefit from higher reputation, attracts MNCs, and better standing or power in international conferences such as the IMF. Such firms can expand, increasing job opportunities, reducing unemployment rate, and poverty; its high profits give governments high tax revenue which can be spent on education to increase the productivity of the country. However, if all private sector clothes firms merge, there may be monopolies and if unregulated, cause market failure. Higher market share increases their ability to set high prices as price makers, reducing people's ability to purchase clothes, which is a necessity, reducing living standards as they'll have no substitutes to switch to of lower prices, consumer choice, and as PED is inelastic, monopolistic clothes can exploit consumers. Moreover, the clothing firm may lack incentive to be efficient, increasing production costs which they pass on consumers, reducing productive potential of the country; especially as they use higher inputs to create lower quality goods, causing misallocation of resources which could've been used to create other goods. This lowers output of country, decreasing economic growth. Furthermore its high prices and low quality decreases international competitiveness, reducing exports demanded, causing a BOP deficit and poor current account position due to lower trade in goods, failing a government's macroeconomic goal. Lastly if all the clothing firms merge, they may face diseconomies of scale from growing too large. This causes miscommunication as there's higher levels of management needed, so slow or no reactions to changes in consumer demands and trends, reducing sales and profitability. There's less employee motivation, reducing productivity while increasing costs, potentially leading to inflation if the clothes industry consists of one firm. These higher production costs, if not placed burden on consumers as PED is elastic due to high imports of low priced foreign clothes could cause the firm to go bankrupt. This will cause high unemployment, lowering living standards, especially in countries where its labor-intensive as its the source of many low income people's income, causing high poverty rates. It increases government spending on pensions and unemployment benefits, causing a budget deficit as there's no clothing firms that gives them high tax revenue now, an opportunity cost.
